## Thesis

[AR] The text treats organizational behaviour as a multilevel, contingent system. Individual characteristics, group relationships, tasks and technology, organizational design, organizational processes, and management interact to shape individual, group, and organizational effectiveness; no single variable adequately explains performance. (Ch. 1, “A Model of Organizational Behavior and Management”)

[AR] Its central managerial problem is alignment: matching people with work, rewards with desired behaviour, structures with environments, leadership with followers and situations, and change methods with the nature of the change. Misalignment appears as alienation, ambiguous roles, inequity, conflict, low performance, stress, withdrawal, or organizational decline. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Work”; Ch. 2, “Individual and Cultural Factors in Employee Performance”; Ch. 7, “Work Motivation for Performance”; Ch. 15, “The Internal Organization and External Environments”; Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”)

[AR] Management is consequently presented as both analytical and relational: managers plan, organize, direct, and control resources, but effectiveness also depends on perception, communication, motivation, leadership, political judgement, conflict management, and the capacity to develop people and organizations. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Management”)

[AR] The text repeatedly rejects universal prescriptions. Motivation theories illuminate different mechanisms; leadership effectiveness depends on traits, behaviour, followers, tasks, and context; organizational structures fit different environments; and change methodologies must be selected or combined according to the situation. (Ch. 7, “Motivation: Direction and Intensity”; Ch. 12, “Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”; Ch. 15, “Organizational Designs and Structures”; Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[AR] Appendix A supplies the epistemic foundation for these claims: theory organizes and explains observations, generates testable hypotheses, and is refined through controlled inquiry. Managerial practice should therefore be informed by evidence while remaining attentive to external validity, cost, context, and the limits of any research design. (Appendix A, “Theory Building in Organizations”; Appendix A, “Scientific Method in Organizational Behavior Research”; Appendix A, “Basic Research Designs”)

## 1. Management and organizational behaviour

### Work and its significance

> [V] an activity that produces something of value for other people.

(Ch. 1, “The Nature of Work”)

[AP] This definition expands work beyond paid employment and locates it in a social context: work produces utility, even when the activity itself is repetitive, stressful, or unrewarding. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Work”)

[AP] Work serves economic, social, status, identity, self-esteem, and self-actualization functions. Its absence, or work that denies meaningful control and recognition, can produce alienation rather than fulfilment. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Work”)

### The managerial setting

[AP] Contemporary managers face international competition, technological change, demands for quality and effectiveness, changing workforce demographics, new employee expectations, and ethical pressures. These forces make the effective management of people central to organizational performance. (Ch. 1, “The Changing Workplace”)

[AP] Management is the process of planning, organizing, directing, and controlling employee activities in combination with other resources to accomplish organizational objectives. The definition makes coordination, rather than individual action alone, the distinguishing feature of management. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Management”)

[AP] The text identifies nine managerial responsibilities: long-range planning, controlling, environmental scanning, supervision, coordination, customer relations and marketing, community relations, internal consulting, and monitoring products and services. Their relative importance varies by managerial level and function. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Management”)

[AP] Executive, middle, and first-line managers differ in scope and time horizon. Technical skills matter most near operating work, conceptual skills become increasingly important at higher levels, and human skills remain important throughout the hierarchy. (Ch. 1, “The Nature of Management”)

### Organizational behaviour as a field

[AP] Organizational behaviour studies people’s behaviour within organizations at individual, group, and organizational levels. Micro-organizational behaviour emphasizes individuals and groups, while macro-organizational behaviour addresses organization-wide structures and processes. (Ch. 1, “A Model of Organizational Behavior and Management”)

[AP] The field draws from psychology, sociology, anthropology, economics, and political science. These disciplines illuminate different parts of the same system rather than supplying a single complete explanation. (Ch. 1, “A Model of Organizational Behavior and Management”)

[AR] The text’s organizing model has five building blocks: individuals and groups; tasks and technology; organizational design; organizational processes; and management. These inputs and processes are evaluated through individual, group, and organizational effectiveness. (Ch. 1, “A Model of Organizational Behavior and Management”)

## 2. Individual and cultural differences

### Ability, personality, and performance

[AR] Employee performance depends jointly on ability and motivation. Ability without effort, or effort without the relevant capacity, is insufficient; selection, training, job design, and motivation therefore address different performance constraints. (Ch. 2, “Individual and Cultural Factors in Employee Performance”)

[AP] Ability includes mental, physical, and psychomotor capacities. Cognitive complexity describes a person’s capacity to perceive distinctions and relationships within complex information and can affect how flexibly that person responds to ambiguous managerial problems. (Ch. 2, “Employee Abilities and Skills”)

[AP] Personality is presented as a relatively stable constellation of characteristics influenced by physiological, cultural, family, social, role, and situational factors. Stability does not mean that behaviour is independent of context. (Ch. 2, “Personality: An Introduction”)

[AP] Work-relevant characteristics discussed include self-esteem, locus of control, introversion and extroversion, authoritarianism, dogmatism, and dependability. These characteristics affect responses to authority, uncertainty, social interaction, feedback, and responsibility. (Ch. 2, “Personality and Work Behavior”)

### Person–organization tension

[BT] The text attributes the basic incongruity thesis to Chris Argyris. It contrasts movement toward adult maturity—greater activity, independence, behavioural variety, deeper interests, longer time perspectives, more equal status, and self-awareness—with traditional organizational conditions that favour passivity, dependence, narrow behaviour, shallow interests, short perspectives, subordinate status, and limited self-control. (Ch. 2, “Personality and Organization: A Basic Conflict?”)

[AR] The resulting argument is not that organization is inherently harmful, but that rigid designs can frustrate mature needs. More participative, responsible, and varied work can reduce this conflict. (Ch. 2, “Personality and Organization: A Basic Conflict?”)

### Values, ethics, and culture

[BT] The text attributes the distinction between terminal and instrumental values to Milton Rokeach. Terminal values describe desired end states; instrumental values describe preferred ways of behaving. Values guide choices, influence perceptions, and provide standards for evaluating conduct. (Ch. 2, “Personal Values and Ethics”)

[AP] Ethics concerns the standards by which actions are judged right or wrong. Because values differ, ethical judgement cannot be inferred merely from organizational position or cultural familiarity. (Ch. 2, “Personal Values and Ethics”)

[AP] Culture is described as collective mental programming that distinguishes groups. It affects assumptions about authority, work, relationships, time, space, and appropriate behaviour. (Ch. 2, “Cultural Differences”)

[BT] Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck’s framework is presented through six value orientations: the nature of people, people’s relationship to nature, interpersonal relationships, preferred activity, time orientation, and use of space. (Ch. 2, “Cultural Differences”)

## 3. Perception and job attitudes

### Perception as selection and construction

[AP] Perception is not a passive copy of reality. People selectively attend to stimuli, organize them into patterns, and interpret them through prior experience, expectations, needs, and current circumstances. (Ch. 3, “The Perceptual Process”)

[AP] Social perception depends on characteristics of the person observed, the situation, and the perceiver. Physical appearance, verbal and nonverbal communication, and ascribed attributes can shape impressions before task-relevant evidence is considered. (Ch. 3, “The Perceptual Process”)

[AP] Halo and horn effects generalize from one favourable or unfavourable characteristic to an overall judgement. They become especially consequential when impressions affect hiring, appraisal, promotion, or access to responsibility. (Ch. 3, “The Perceptual Process”)

### Barriers and attribution

[AP] The text identifies three major barriers to accurate social perception: stereotyping, selective perception, and perceptual defence. Perceptual defence can operate through denial, modification and distortion, changed recognition, or recognition accompanied by refusal to change. (Ch. 3, “Barriers to Accurate Social Perception”)

[BT] Attribution theory is introduced through Fritz Heider’s distinction between internal and external causes of behaviour. The observer decides whether an action reflects the person or surrounding circumstances. (Ch. 3, “Attributions: Interpreting the Causes of Behavior”)

[BT] Harold Kelley’s model uses consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness to infer causation. High consensus, high distinctiveness, and low consistency support an external attribution; low consensus, low distinctiveness, and high consistency favour an internal one. (Ch. 3, “Attributions: Interpreting the Causes of Behavior”)

[AP] The fundamental attribution error overweights personal causes when explaining others’ behaviour, while self-serving bias tends to credit personal qualities for success and external conditions for failure. (Ch. 3, “Attributions: Interpreting the Causes of Behavior”)

### Attitudes at work

[AP] Attitudes contain cognitive, affective, and behavioural-intention components. Behaviour and attitudes can influence one another, and inconsistency can generate pressure for cognitive adjustment or behavioural justification. (Ch. 3, “Attitudes and Behavior”)

[AP] Job involvement concerns psychological identification with work; organizational commitment concerns attachment to the organization; job satisfaction is an affective evaluation of one’s job and its characteristics. (Ch. 3, “Work-Related Attitudes”)

[AP] The text discusses five dimensions of job satisfaction: the work itself, pay, promotion opportunities, supervision, and coworkers. The Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire expands measurement into twenty-six scales. (Ch. 3, “Work-Related Attitudes”)

## 4. Learning and reinforcement

### Learning models

[AP] Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience. The text traces four major approaches: classical conditioning, the law of effect, operant conditioning, and social learning. (Ch. 4, “Basic Models of Learning”)

[BT] Pavlov’s classical-conditioning work links a previously neutral stimulus to an elicited response. Thorndike’s law of effect holds that consequences influence whether behaviour recurs, while Skinner’s operant model focuses directly on controlling consequences. (Ch. 4, “Basic Models of Learning”)

[BT] Albert Bandura’s social-learning account uses reciprocal determinism: behaviour, the person, and the environment influence one another. Observational learning depends on attention, retention, behavioural reproduction, and an incentive to perform. (Ch. 4, “Basic Models of Learning”)

[AP] Learning effectiveness is influenced by motivation, knowledge of results or feedback, prior learning, whether material is learned as a whole or in parts, and whether practice is massed or distributed. (Ch. 4, “Basic Models of Learning”)

### Consequences and schedules

[AP] Positive reinforcement presents a desirable consequence; avoidance or negative reinforcement removes an undesirable condition; extinction withholds reinforcement; punishment presents an adverse consequence or removes something valued. (Ch. 4, “Reinforcement and Behavioral Change”)

[AP] Partial reinforcement may follow fixed-interval, fixed-ratio, variable-interval, or variable-ratio schedules. These schedules differ in whether reinforcement depends on time or responses and whether the requirement is predictable or variable. (Ch. 4, “Reinforcement and Behavioral Change”)

[AR] The text treats reinforcement as consequential but not mechanically sufficient. Prior learning, cognition, delayed consequences, perceived fairness, and the possibility of unintended behaviour complicate attempts to control behaviour through rewards or punishment. (Ch. 4, “Reinforcement and Behavioral Change”)

### Planned and self-directed change

[AP] Organizational behaviour modification proceeds through identifying critical behaviour, measuring its baseline, analysing antecedents and consequences, intervening, and evaluating performance change. (Ch. 4, “Behavior Modification in Organizations”)

[BT] David Kolb’s experiential-learning cycle moves through concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. (Ch. 4, “Behavior Modification in Organizations”)

[AP] Behavioural self-management transfers observation, goal setting, consequence management, and evaluation to the individual. It combines behavioural techniques with self-regulation, self-reinforcement, and cognitive supports such as symbolic coding and self-talk. (Ch. 4, “Behavioral Self-Management”)

[AE] An attendance programme illustrates the approach: employees set attendance goals, monitor their behaviour, arrange personally meaningful reinforcers, and compare later attendance with the baseline. (Ch. 4, “Behavioral Self-Management”)

## 5. Diversity in organizations

### Forms and identities

[AP] Diversity refers to identity-based differences among people, while inclusion concerns whether people are accepted, supported, and able to participate. Representation alone therefore does not establish inclusion. (Ch. 5, “An Introduction to Workplace Diversity”)

[AP] Surface-level diversity involves readily observable differences; deep-level diversity includes values, attitudes, and beliefs; hidden diversity includes identities or experiences not immediately visible. (Ch. 5, “An Introduction to Workplace Diversity”)

[AP] The text examines sex and gender, race and ethnicity, age, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration and work-visa status, disability, religion, and other identities. It distinguishes access discrimination in entry from treatment discrimination after organizational entry. (Ch. 5, “Diversity and the Workforce”; Ch. 5, “Challenges of Diversity”)

### Legal and organizational context

[AP] The U.S. legal discussion covers Title VII, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Equal Pay Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, and the Family and Medical Leave Act. The text treats legal compliance as a floor rather than a complete diversity strategy. (Ch. 5, “Challenges of Diversity”)

[AP] Sexual harassment is distinguished as quid pro quo harassment or a hostile work environment. The glass ceiling names an invisible barrier that restricts advancement despite formal access. (Ch. 5, “Diversity and the Workforce”; Ch. 5, “Challenges of Diversity”)

### Organizational effects and interpretive frameworks

[BT] Cox and Blake identify six possible competitive opportunities from effectively managed diversity: cost, resource acquisition, marketing, system flexibility, creativity, and problem solving. These are opportunities rather than automatic outcomes. (Ch. 5, “Diversity and Its Impact on Companies”)

[AP] The resource-based view frames diversity as a possible advantage when associated capabilities are valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and not readily substitutable. The advantage depends on organizational practices that convert differences into usable knowledge and relationships. (Ch. 5, “Diversity and Its Impact on Companies”)

[AP] Similarity-attraction, social identity, schema, cognitive-diversity, and justification-suppression perspectives explain why diversity can affect attraction, categorization, information processing, prejudice, conflict, and performance in different ways. (Ch. 5, “Key Diversity Theories”)

[BT] Ely and Thomas distinguish integration-and-learning, access-and-legitimacy, and discrimination-and-fairness perspectives. The integration-and-learning perspective incorporates different experiences into core work rather than treating diversity only as market access or equal treatment. (Ch. 5, “Key Diversity Theories”)

[AR] Diversity has no unconditional performance effect in the text. Outcomes depend on task requirements, leadership, inclusion, conflict, organizational culture, and whether differences become sources of knowledge or bases for division. (Ch. 5, “Benefits and Challenges of Workplace Diversity”)

[AP] Recommendations include leadership commitment, accountability, recruitment beyond familiar networks, structured selection, mentoring, development, work–life support, attention to climate, and ongoing measurement. The text lists fifteen characteristics of highly structured interviews intended to improve consistency and reduce demographic similarity effects. (Ch. 5, “Recommendations for Managing Diversity”)

## 6. Perception and managerial decision-making

### Decision processes and types

[AP] Decision-making is the process of considering possible options and selecting one. Managerial decisions affect multiple stakeholders and are shaped by information, emotion, organizational responsibilities, and ethical consequences. (Ch. 6, “Overview of Managerial Decision-Making”)

[AP] Reflective processing is deliberate, logical, and conscious; reactive processing is fast, intuitive, and emotionally influenced. Effective judgement may use both, with emotional intelligence helping decision makers recognize and regulate affect. (Ch. 6, “How the Brain Processes Information to Make Decisions: Reflective and Reactive Systems”)

[AP] Programmed decisions address recurring, sufficiently understood problems through established rules or procedures. Nonprogrammed decisions concern novel, ambiguous, or consequential situations that require judgement and new alternatives. (Ch. 6, “Programmed and Nonprogrammed Decisions”)

[AP] The six-step decision process is to recognize a decision is needed, generate alternatives, analyse them, select one, implement it, and evaluate its effectiveness. Evaluation can reveal a need to revise the chosen action or the original framing. (Ch. 6, “Overview of Managerial Decision-Making”)

### Barriers and improvement

[AP] Bounded rationality, escalation of commitment, time pressure, uncertainty, biases, and conflict limit decision quality. Satisficing selects an acceptable rather than demonstrably optimal alternative when information or processing capacity is constrained. (Ch. 6, “Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”)

[AP] Confirmation bias favours evidence consistent with existing beliefs. Escalation of commitment continues a failing course because of prior investments, responsibility, or reluctance to acknowledge error. (Ch. 6, “Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”)

[AP] Process conflict concerns how work should be performed; relationship conflict concerns interpersonal tension. The former may sometimes improve deliberation, whereas the latter more readily diverts attention and damages cooperation. (Ch. 6, “Barriers to Effective Decision-Making”)

[AP] The text identifies seven reasoning errors: non sequitur, false cause, ad hominem, the genetic fallacy, appeal to tradition, bandwagon reasoning, and appeal to emotion. Critical thinking asks whether conclusions follow from relevant and sufficient evidence. (Ch. 6, “Improving the Quality of Decision-Making”)

[BT] James Rest’s ethical-decision model requires ethical sensitivity, moral judgement, moral motivation or intention, and the character or action capacity to carry the decision through. Recognizing an ethical issue is therefore only one part of ethical conduct. (Ch. 6, “Improving the Quality of Decision-Making”)

### Group decisions

[AP] Groups can contribute broader knowledge, more alternatives, error detection, and acceptance of implementation. They also impose time costs and risks from conformity, domination, suppressed dissent, social pressure, and groupthink. (Ch. 6, “Group Decision-Making”)

[AP] Brainstorming, devil’s advocacy, and deliberate protection of dissent are presented as ways to expand alternatives and test assumptions, provided the group does not treat formal participation as evidence that members were genuinely heard. (Ch. 6, “Group Decision-Making”)

## 7. Work motivation for performance

### Motivation and performance

[AP] Performance depends on ability, effort or motivation, accurate role perceptions, and a supportive performance environment. A severe deficiency in one cannot necessarily be compensated for by abundance in another. (Ch. 7, “Motivation: Direction and Intensity”)

[AP] Motivation is a force within or outside the person that energizes, directs, and sustains behaviour. Work motivation concerns both direction—what effort is aimed at—and intensity—how much effort is applied. (Ch. 7, “Motivation: Direction and Intensity”)

> [V] there is no “one best theory.”

(Ch. 7, “Motivation: Direction and Intensity”)

[AR] Content theories ask what needs energize behaviour; process theories explain how choices, goals, consequences, comparisons, and expectations translate into effort. The theories are treated as complementary lenses rather than mutually exclusive doctrines. (Ch. 7, “Motivation: Direction and Intensity”)

### Needs and content theories

[BT] Henry Murray’s manifest-needs approach distinguishes primary and secondary needs and treats their relative strength as varying across people. (Ch. 7, “Content Theories of Motivation”)

[BT] McClelland and Atkinson’s learned-needs account emphasizes achievement, affiliation, and power. High achievement need is associated with personal responsibility, moderate risk, and clear performance feedback; power can be pursued for personal dominance or social and organizational purposes. (Ch. 7, “Content Theories of Motivation”)

[BT] Maslow’s hierarchy orders physiological, safety, social, esteem, and self-actualization needs. The text presents the hierarchy as influential while noting weak support for a rigid sequence. (Ch. 7, “Content Theories of Motivation”)

[BT] Alderfer’s ERG theory condenses needs into existence, relatedness, and growth. Satisfaction progression, frustration, frustration regression, and aspiration allow movement in more than one direction. (Ch. 7, “Content Theories of Motivation”)

[BT] Herzberg distinguishes motivators associated with job content and satisfaction from hygiene factors associated with job context and dissatisfaction. Satisfaction and dissatisfaction are treated as separate continua, so removing a hygiene problem does not necessarily motivate. (Ch. 7, “Content Theories of Motivation”)

[AP] Self-determination theory emphasizes competence, autonomy, and relatedness. External controls can support action but may also crowd out intrinsic motivation when they undermine autonomy. (Ch. 7, “Content Theories of Motivation”)

### Process theories

[AP] Operant conditioning links behaviour to consequences; equity theory links motivation to perceived input–outcome ratios; goal theory links performance to goal properties and commitment; expectancy theory links effort to expected performance and valued outcomes. (Ch. 7, “Process Theories of Motivation”)

[BT] Adams’s equity model compares one’s inputs and outcomes with a referent. Perceived underreward or overreward can prompt changes in inputs, outcomes, perceptions, referents, the other person, or membership in the situation. (Ch. 7, “Process Theories of Motivation”)

[AP] Goal effects are strongest when goals are specific, difficult but attainable, accepted, and supported by commitment and feedback. Self-set, participatively set, and assigned goals can all work; vague “do your best” goals provide less direction. (Ch. 7, “Process Theories of Motivation”)

[AP] Expectancy theory combines effort-to-performance expectancy, performance-to-outcome expectancy, and outcome valence. Motivation weakens if the person doubts that effort can produce performance, doubts that performance will produce outcomes, or does not value those outcomes. (Ch. 7, “Process Theories of Motivation”)

[AR] Recent research integrates motivation rather than selecting a sole cause: needs affect valued outcomes, goals direct effort, self-efficacy affects expectancy, reinforcement changes consequences, and organizational justice affects whether the system is accepted. (Ch. 7, “Recent Research on Motivation Theories”)

## 8. Performance appraisal and rewards

### Appraisal purposes and quality

[AP] Performance appraisal evaluates work, communicates feedback, and informs discretionary rewards or decisions. The text identifies five uses: performance feedback, employee self-development, reward allocation, personnel decisions, and identification of training and development needs. (Ch. 8, “Performance Appraisal Systems”)

[AP] Validity asks whether an appraisal measures relevant performance; reliability asks whether measurement is consistent. Neither is guaranteed merely because a form is standardized or numerical. (Ch. 8, “Performance Appraisal Systems”)

[AP] Five recurring appraisal errors are central tendency, strictness or leniency, halo effects, recency, and personal bias. These errors can distort both development and reward decisions. (Ch. 8, “Performance Appraisal Systems”)

### Techniques and feedback

[AP] Six appraisal techniques are examined: graphic rating scales, critical incidents, behaviourally anchored rating scales, behavioural observation scales, management by objectives, and assessment centres. Their relative usefulness depends on purpose, cost, observability, and the kind of performance being assessed. (Ch. 8, “Techniques of Performance Appraisal”)

[AP] Effective feedback depends on its source, accuracy, credibility, perceived fairness, consistency with expectations, and reasonableness. Feedback is less useful when recipients cannot connect it to observable behaviour or feasible action. (Ch. 8, “Feedback”)

### Reward systems

[AP] Reward systems influence effort and performance, attendance and retention, organizational commitment, satisfaction, and occupational or organizational choice. Their signals extend beyond the monetary value of a particular payment. (Ch. 8, “Reward Systems in Organizations”)

[BT] Lawler’s account distinguishes the amount of reward received, the amount believed deserved, comparison with others, and the value attached to different rewards. Satisfaction depends on perception and comparison, not reward quantity alone. (Ch. 8, “Reward Systems in Organizations”)

[AP] Rewards may be distributed according to power, equality, need, or distributive justice. Each basis communicates a different rationale and can produce different perceptions of legitimacy. (Ch. 8, “Reward Systems in Organizations”)

[AP] Money can provide purchasing power, status, comparison, security, and influence. Its motivational effect depends on whether pay is important to the employee, performance differences are measurable, performance actually changes pay, and the relationship is understood. (Ch. 8, “Reward Systems in Organizations”)

[AR] Pay secrecy protects privacy and managerial discretion but can obstruct trust and accurate comparison. Transparent systems can improve understanding while exposing inconsistency or inequity. (Ch. 8, “Reward Systems in Organizations”)

[AP] Individual incentives can strengthen line-of-sight between effort and reward but may undermine cooperation. Group incentives support interdependence but can create measurement problems and free riding. (Ch. 8, “Individual and Group Incentive Plans”)

[AP] Alternatives discussed include gain sharing, skill-based incentives, lump-sum increases, participative pay decisions, and flexible benefits. Their effectiveness depends on strategic fit, employee value, performance information, credibility, and administrative capacity. (Ch. 8, “Individual and Group Incentive Plans”)

## 9. Group and intergroup relations

### Group formation and structure

[AP] A group consists of people who interact, share norms or roles, and pursue common purposes. Formal and informal groups may be permanent or temporary, producing command, task, friendship, and interest groups. (Ch. 9, “Work Groups: Basic Considerations”)

[AP] People join groups for security, social needs, esteem, economic self-interest, mutual interest, and physical proximity. A single group can satisfy several motives simultaneously. (Ch. 9, “Work Groups: Basic Considerations”)

[BT] Tuckman’s model presents forming, storming, norming, and performing as developmental stages. They describe recurring group problems rather than a guarantee that every group advances smoothly. (Ch. 9, “Work Groups: Basic Considerations”)

[AP] Group structure is analysed through roles, size, norms, status, and cohesiveness. Each channels behaviour independently of formal job descriptions. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

### Roles, norms, and cohesion

[AP] Task roles advance the work, relationship roles maintain the group, and self-oriented roles serve individual needs. A role episode moves from expectations, to communicated role pressures, to perceived expectations, to enacted behaviour. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

[AP] Role conflict occurs when expectations are incompatible; role ambiguity when expectations are unclear; role overload when demands exceed time or capacity. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

[AP] Larger groups possess more resources but face coordination and participation losses. Social loafing can arise when individual contributions are difficult to identify, members expect others to reduce effort, or outcomes seem disconnected from personal effort. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

[AP] Norms regulate important behaviour, simplify choices, support group survival, express values, and help predict others’ actions. The same mechanisms can sustain high performance or enforce restriction of output. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

[BT] The text uses Solomon Asch’s conformity experiments to show that unanimous group pressure can alter publicly stated judgements even on comparatively clear tasks. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

[AP] Status may arise from birth, personal characteristics, achievement, possessions, or formal authority. Status systems can motivate, support identification and dignity, and stabilize interaction, but incongruence can generate conflict. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

[AP] Cohesiveness is influenced by member similarity, group maturity, size, interaction frequency, clear goals, external threat, and prior success. Its performance effect depends on whether group norms support organizational goals. (Ch. 9, “Work Group Structure”)

### Effectiveness and interdependence

[BT] Hackman evaluates groups through productive output, satisfaction of member needs, and capacity for future cooperation. Immediate output alone can therefore conceal damage to members or future viability. (Ch. 9, “Managing Effective Work Groups”)

[BT] Hackman’s performance account centres on effort, member knowledge and skill, and task-performance strategy, supported or constrained by organizational context, group design, and interpersonal processes. (Ch. 9, “Managing Effective Work Groups”)

[AP] Intergroup work creates requirements for interdependence, information flow, and integration. Pooled, sequential, and reciprocal interdependence demand progressively more intensive coordination. (Ch. 9, “Intergroup Behavior and Performance”)

[AP] Coordination mechanisms include rules, direct exchange, linking roles, task forces, and decoupling. The mechanism should match the frequency, uncertainty, and reciprocity of the dependency. (Ch. 9, “Intergroup Behavior and Performance”)

## 10. Understanding and managing work teams

### What makes a team

[BT] Katzenbach and Smith distinguish a team from a working group through common commitment and purpose, specific performance goals, complementary skills, commitment to a common working method, and mutual accountability. (Ch. 10, “Teamwork in the Workplace”)

[AR] A working group can coordinate individual outputs without becoming a team. Team performance requires members to accept collective responsibility for a shared product or result. (Ch. 10, “Teamwork in the Workplace”)

[AP] Practices supporting team formation include urgency and direction, careful attention to skills, constructive first meetings, clear ground rules, early performance-oriented tasks, fresh information, time together, and positive feedback and reward. (Ch. 10, “Teamwork in the Workplace”)

[BT] Gratton and Erickson’s collaboration research identifies eight organizational factors, including executive support, relationship-oriented practices, modelling collaboration, a gift culture, community, strong leadership, role clarity, and task clarity. (Ch. 10, “Teamwork in the Workplace”)

### Development and managerial paradoxes

[BT] The chapter gives Tuckman’s original 1965 sequence of forming, storming, norming, and performing and notes the later addition of adjourning. It cautions that real team development can loop or regress rather than proceed linearly. (Ch. 10, “Team Development Over Time”)

[AR] Team managers must hold several tensions: individual and collective needs, support and confrontation, performance and learning, and managerial authority and team autonomy. Excessive resolution toward either pole weakens the other requirement. (Ch. 10, “Things to Consider When Managing Teams”)

[AP] The manager, team, and individual form an interdependent triangle. Boundaries require active management because information, resources, authority, and expectations cross between the team and its environment. (Ch. 10, “Things to Consider When Managing Teams”)

### Conflict, trust, and diversity

[AP] Conflict can improve a team when it exposes assumptions and enables learning. Avoidance can preserve surface harmony while allowing substantive disagreement to remain unresolved. (Ch. 10, “Opportunities and Challenges to Team Building”)

[BT] Patrick Lencioni’s account places absence of trust beneath fear of conflict. The text presents “mining” for buried disagreement and granting real-time permission to challenge as ways of making conflict discussable. (Ch. 10, “Opportunities and Challenges to Team Building”)

[AR] Diverse teams can access broader information and perspectives but may initially face communication, trust, and coordination costs. Leadership and inclusive processes determine whether difference becomes insight or fragmentation. (Ch. 10, “Team Diversity”)

[AP] Multicultural teams may differ in direct versus indirect communication, accents and fluency, attitudes toward hierarchy, and decision-making norms. Possible interventions are adaptation, structural intervention, managerial intervention, and exit. (Ch. 10, “Multicultural Teams”)

[AP] Cultural intelligence combines knowledge, mindful interpretation, and behavioural capability. The chapter characterizes these as head, body, and heart: understanding, acting appropriately, and sustaining confidence and motivation. (Ch. 10, “Multicultural Teams”)

## 11. Communication

### Communication as a process

[AP] Managerial communication begins when a communicator encodes meaning into a message and a receiver decodes it. Feedback closes the loop, while noise can enter through language, channel, attention, assumptions, relationships, or context. (Ch. 11, “The Process of Managerial Communication”)

[AP] Feedback can be informational, corrective, or reinforcing. Its function is not merely to confirm reception but to reveal what the receiver understood and how future action should change. (Ch. 11, “The Process of Managerial Communication”)

[AP] Oral, written, and nonverbal communication differ in speed, persistence, richness, documentation, and exposure to ambiguity. Channel choice should reflect the complexity, sensitivity, and permanence of the message. (Ch. 11, “Types of Communications in Organizations”)

### Social and managerial context

[AP] Communication is influenced by social relationships, perception, interaction involvement, and organizational design. Interaction involvement includes responsiveness, perceptiveness, and attentiveness. (Ch. 11, “Factors Affecting Communications and the Roles of Managers”)

[BT] Mintzberg’s managerial roles are grouped as interpersonal—figurehead, leader, liaison; informational—monitor, disseminator, spokesperson; and decisional—entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator. Communication is the medium through which these roles operate. (Ch. 11, “Factors Affecting Communications and the Roles of Managers”)

[AP] Corporate identity concerns how an organization understands and presents itself; reputation concerns how others evaluate it. Managerial language, responsiveness, consistency, and visible action affect the relationship between them. (Ch. 11, “Managerial Communication and Corporate Reputation”)

> [V] Information never speaks for itself.

(Ch. 11, “The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)

[AR] Meaning is socially constructed: the same information can produce different interpretations depending on context, messenger, framing, prior relationships, and assumptions about intent. (Ch. 11, “The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)

[AP] Talking, listening, reading, and writing are the principal managerial channels. Writing forces precision and leaves a persistent record; listening is an active process of attention and interpretation rather than silent waiting. (Ch. 11, “The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing”)

[AP] Organizational communication also flows downward, upward, and horizontally. The direction affects what information is available, what risks accompany candour, and how quickly coordination occurs. (Ch. 11, “Summary of Learning Outcomes”)

---

## 12. Leadership

### Leadership, management, and followers

[AP] Leadership is a social influence relationship directed toward mutual goals. Groups require both task functions and maintenance functions, whether these are supplied by a formally appointed manager or an emergent leader. (Ch. 12, “The Nature of Leadership”)

[AR] Management and leadership overlap but are not identical. Appointment grants formal authority; leadership can emerge through influence. Management often relies on legitimate and extrinsic controls, while leadership can evoke identification and intrinsic commitment. Organizations need both coordination and direction. (Ch. 12, “The Nature of Leadership”)

[AP] The leadership process comprises leaders, followers, context, influence processes, and consequences. Followers are active participants whose needs, skills, interpretations, and responses partly create leadership outcomes. (Ch. 12, “The Leadership Process”)

[AP] Leader–member exchange focuses on distinct dyadic relationships. Higher-quality exchanges tend to involve greater trust, support, and latitude, while lower-quality exchanges are more restricted to formal role requirements. (Ch. 12, “The Leadership Process”)

### Emergence and power

[AP] Formal leaders are designated by the organization; informal leaders emerge from interaction. A person may become influential because others depend on their expertise, relationships, initiative, or access to critical resources. (Ch. 12, “Leader Emergence”)

[BT] Salancik and Pfeffer’s resource perspective explains emergence through control of scarce, critical organizational resources. Influence follows dependency rather than title alone. (Ch. 12, “Leader Emergence”)

[BT] French and Raven’s five power bases are reward, coercive, referent, expert, and legitimate power. Referent and expert power are more closely associated with commitment; legitimate and reward power commonly produce compliance; coercive power readily produces resistance. (Ch. 12, “Leader Emergence”)

### Styles, traits, and behaviour

[BT] Tannenbaum and Schmidt arrange leadership along a continuum from manager-centred authority to subordinate-centred freedom. The appropriate position depends on the manager, subordinates, and situation. (Ch. 12, “The Trait Approach to Leadership”)

[BT] McGregor’s Theory X assumes employees require direction and control, while Theory Y assumes work can be natural and people can exercise self-direction under suitable conditions. These assumptions influence managerial behaviour. (Ch. 12, “The Trait Approach to Leadership”)

[BT] Muczyk and Reimann combine directive versus permissive decision execution with autocratic versus democratic decision formation, producing directive autocrat, permissive autocrat, directive democrat, and permissive democrat patterns. (Ch. 12, “The Trait Approach to Leadership”)

[BT] Stogdill’s reviews undermine the search for a single universal trait profile. The text nevertheless reports recurring traits such as drive, leadership motivation, honesty and integrity, self-confidence, cognitive ability, and business knowledge, while stressing situational expression. (Ch. 12, “The Trait Approach to Leadership”)

[AP] Ohio State research distinguishes consideration from initiating structure. Michigan work contrasts job-centred and employee-centred leadership and identifies support, work facilitation, goal emphasis, and interaction facilitation. (Ch. 12, “Behavioral Approaches to Leadership”)

[BT] Blake and Mouton’s grid combines concern for production with concern for people. The text cautions against assuming that the high–high style is universally superior. (Ch. 12, “Behavioral Approaches to Leadership”)

### Contingency and newer leadership forms

[BT] Fiedler’s contingency model matches a leader’s least-preferred-coworker orientation with leader–member relations, task structure, and position power. Effectiveness follows fit rather than wholesale conversion of leader style. (Ch. 12, “Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)

[BT] Path–goal theory gives supportive, directive, participative, and achievement-oriented behaviours. Leaders clarify paths, remove obstacles, and connect performance with valued goals according to follower and task characteristics. (Ch. 12, “Situational (Contingency) Approaches to Leadership”)

[AP] Follower characteristics, task properties, and organizational arrangements may substitute for leadership or neutralize a leader’s influence. Professional competence, intrinsically satisfying tasks, cohesive groups, formal rules, or distance can reduce the effect of direct leadership. (Ch. 12, “Substitutes for and Neutralizers of Leadership”)

[AP] Transactional leadership exchanges rewards for agreed performance. Transformational leadership operates through charisma, individualized consideration, intellectual stimulation, and inspirational motivation; visionary leadership articulates a credible desired future. (Ch. 12, “Transformational, Visionary, and Charismatic Leadership”)

[BT] The text invokes Max Weber when defining charisma as an extraordinary quality attributed to a leader by followers. Charisma is therefore relational and perceptual, not simply a self-declared trait. (Ch. 12, “Transformational, Visionary, and Charismatic Leadership”)

[AR] Future leadership needs include strategic and global judgement, opportunity recognition, work in decentralized systems, competence with diversity, strong interpersonal capability, and responsibility to wider communities. (Ch. 12, “Leadership Needs in the 21st Century”)

## 13. Organizational power and politics

### Power, authority, and dependency

[AP] Power is the capacity to affect others’ behaviour; authority is institutionally sanctioned power; leadership is influence directed toward shared goals. The concepts overlap without being interchangeable. (Ch. 13, “Power in Interpersonal Relations”)

[BT] Etzioni distinguishes coercive, utilitarian, and normative power. French and Raven’s reward, coercive, legitimate, referent, and expert bases provide a more interpersonal classification. (Ch. 13, “Power in Interpersonal Relations”)

[AP] Responses to power range from commitment through compliance to resistance. The response depends on the power base, perceived legitimacy, relationship, values, and available counterpower. (Ch. 13, “Power in Interpersonal Relations”)

[AR] Power rests on dependency. Dependency grows when a resource is important, scarce, or difficult to replace; counterpower grows when the nominally less powerful party controls something the other needs. (Ch. 13, “Power in Interpersonal Relations”)

### Use and ethics of power

[AP] Seven influence tactics are emphasized: controlling information, controlling access to people, selectively using objective criteria, controlling agendas, using outside experts, bureaucratic gamesmanship, and building coalitions. (Ch. 13, “Uses of Power”)

[AP] Offices, titles, access, symbols, schedules, and participation in important decisions can signal power, but symbols need not correspond perfectly with actual dependency or influence. (Ch. 13, “Uses of Power”)

[AR] Ethical power use requires considering legitimate organizational purposes, affected parties, procedural fairness, accurate information, and whether the tactic could be publicly defended. Power itself is not treated as inherently unethical. (Ch. 13, “Uses of Power”)

### Political behaviour

[AP] Politics is power in action: activity through which individuals or groups pursue preferred outcomes where interests differ. It can serve organizational goals or private advantage. (Ch. 13, “Political Behavior in Organizations”)

[AP] Political activity intensifies when uncertainty and complexity are high and resources are contested. Ambiguous goals, scarce resources, changing technology or environments, nonprogrammed decisions, and organizational change are especially favourable conditions. (Ch. 13, “Political Behavior in Organizations”)

[AP] Resource-dependence and strategic-contingency accounts explain departmental power through the capacity to cope with uncertainty, lack of substitutes, and centrality. Centrality includes both workflow pervasiveness and workflow immediacy. (Ch. 13, “Political Behavior in Organizations”)

[AP] The text proposes four broad ways to limit destructive politics: reduce uncertainty, reduce resource competition, break existing political fiefdoms, and prevent new fiefdoms from consolidating. (Ch. 13, “Limiting the Influence of Political Behavior”)

---

## 14. Conflict and negotiations

### Nature, levels, and consequences

[AP] Conflict begins when goal-directed behaviour is blocked or perceived to be blocked. It may concern incompatible goals, ideas, emotions, or overt actions. (Ch. 14, “Conflict in Organizations: Basic Considerations”)

[AP] The text distinguishes goal, cognitive, affective, and behavioural conflict, and locates conflict at intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup, and interorganizational levels. (Ch. 14, “Conflict in Organizations: Basic Considerations”)

> [V] Conflict itself is neither good nor bad, productive nor destructive.

(Ch. 14, “Conflict in Organizations: Basic Considerations”)

[AR] Conflict outcomes depend on its level, subject, process, and management. Too little conflict can permit stagnation; moderate conflict can stimulate problem solving and adaptation; excessive or personalized conflict consumes resources and disrupts cooperation. (Ch. 14, “Conflict in Organizations: Basic Considerations”)

### Causes and resolution

[AP] Seven major antecedents are task interdependence, status inconsistency, jurisdictional ambiguity, communication problems, dependence on common resources, differences in performance standards, and individual differences. (Ch. 14, “Causes of Conflict in Organizations”)

[BT] Kenneth Thomas’s process model moves through frustration, conceptualization, behaviour, and outcome. Parties first experience obstruction, form an interpretation, choose behaviour, and then encounter consequences that affect later conflict. (Ch. 14, “Resolving Conflict in Organizations”)

[BT] Thomas’s five modes combine assertiveness with cooperativeness: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating. No mode is always appropriate; urgency, stakes, relationships, information, and power affect the choice. (Ch. 14, “Resolving Conflict in Organizations”)

[AP] Five ineffective approaches are nonaction, administrative orbiting, due-process nonaction, secrecy, and character assassination. These approaches displace, delay, or personalize conflict rather than resolving its causes. (Ch. 14, “Resolving Conflict in Organizations”)

[AP] Preventive measures include superordinate organizational goals, well-structured tasks, intergroup communication, and avoiding unnecessary win–lose conditions. (Ch. 14, “Resolving Conflict in Organizations”)

[AP] Conflict-reduction methods include physical separation, rules and procedures, limiting interaction, integrators, confrontation and negotiation, third-party consultation, member rotation, superordinate goals, and intergroup training. (Ch. 14, “Resolving Conflict in Organizations”)

### Negotiation

[AP] Negotiation commonly moves through non-task relationship building, information exchange, influence and persuasion, and closing. Preparation before these encounters strongly affects what follows. (Ch. 14, “Negotiation Behavior”)

[AP] Distributive bargaining divides a fixed amount and emphasizes resistance points and claims. Integrative bargaining searches for differences in interests, priorities, timing, or risk that allow joint gain. (Ch. 14, “Negotiation Behavior”)

[AR] Effective preparation identifies issues, priorities, target outcomes, resistance points, the other party’s probable position, and alternatives if agreement fails. The text’s key terms attribute principled negotiation and BATNA to Fisher, Ury, and Patton. (Ch. 14, “Negotiation Behavior”; Ch. 14, “Key Terms”)

[AP] Cultural differences can affect relationship building, directness, persuasion, authority, time, emotion, and agreement form. The text presents these as tendencies with substantial within-culture variation, not deterministic national profiles. (Ch. 14, “Negotiation Behavior”)

---

## 15. External and internal organizational environments and corporate culture

### Environmental demands

[AP] Organizations operate amid sociocultural, technological, economic, governmental and political, and natural or human-induced environmental forces. Globalization expands the number and interdependence of relevant actors. (Ch. 15, “The Organization’s External Environment”)

[AP] Contemporary examples include artificial intelligence and digital technologies, cybersecurity, blockchain, sharing-economy models, changing educational credentials, and increased expectations concerning ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility. (Ch. 15, “The Organization’s External Environment”)

[AP] Environmental complexity depends on the number and dissimilarity of external elements; stability depends on their rate and predictability of change. Combining these produces simple-stable, simple-unstable, complex-stable, and complex-unstable environments. (Ch. 15, “External Environments and Industries”)

[AR] Internal complexity can be managed through modular units, simple rules, networks of capability, a common brand, and shared values. These methods seek coordination without requiring every decision to pass through a single hierarchy. (Ch. 15, “External Environments and Industries”)

### Structural responses

[AP] Mechanistic systems emphasize hierarchy, formalization, specialization, centralized authority, and predictable routines. Organic systems emphasize flexibility, decentralization, lateral communication, and adaptation. (Ch. 15, “Organizational Designs and Structures”)

[AP] The text describes three broad structural eras: self-contained organization designs, horizontal organization designs, and open-boundary designs. Each responds to increasing environmental complexity and interdependence. (Ch. 15, “Organizational Designs and Structures”)

[AP] Six major structures are functional, divisional, geographic, matrix, networked-team, and virtual structures. Functional structures support specialization and scale but risk silos; divisional and geographic forms increase market focus but may duplicate resources or fragment the enterprise. (Ch. 15, “Organizational Designs and Structures”)

[AP] Matrix structures coordinate across two dimensions but create multiple authority lines. Networked-team structures enable flexible expertise and rapid response but depend on communication and trust. Virtual structures broaden access to talent and reduce geographic costs while increasing risks of isolation and coordination failure. (Ch. 15, “Organizational Designs and Structures”)

### Alignment and culture

[BT] The open-systems account is associated with Katz and Kahn and with Bertalanffy’s general systems work. Organizations take inputs from the environment, transform them through internal processes, produce outputs, and use feedback to adapt. (Ch. 15, “The Internal Organization and External Environments”)

[AP] An organization’s domain expresses its purpose and helps orient strategy, capabilities, resources, and management systems. Internal and external dimensions must be aligned, but alignment is temporary because environments, leadership, and strategies continue to change. (Ch. 15, “The Internal Organization and External Environments”)

[AP] The McKinsey 7-S model places strategy, structure, systems, skills, staff, and style around shared values. It emphasizes that a change in one internal dimension can require changes in others. (Ch. 15, “The Internal Organization and External Environments”)

[BT] A framework adapted from Lewin and Stephens links environmental scanning and purpose to strategy, organizational capabilities, resources, and management systems. (Ch. 15, “The Internal Organization and External Environments”)

[AP] Organizational culture serves external adaptation and internal integration. Founders and top leaders strongly influence its values and ethical tone, but subcultures can develop among occupations, levels, or units. (Ch. 15, “Corporate Cultures”)

[BT] Cameron and Quinn’s Competing Values Framework combines internal versus external focus with flexibility versus stability and control. It yields adhocracy, clan, hierarchy, and market cultures. (Ch. 15, “Corporate Cultures”)

[AP] Adhocracy emphasizes innovation and experimentation; clan culture emphasizes relationships and development; hierarchy culture emphasizes efficiency, precision, and control; market culture emphasizes competition and results. Large organizations may contain a dominant culture and contrasting subcultures. (Ch. 15, “Corporate Cultures”)

### Emerging demands

[AP] The cited Global Risks Perception Survey highlights persistent inequality, political tension, environmental danger, and cyber vulnerability. The “nine resilience lens” is grouped into structural, integrative, and transformative resilience. (Ch. 15, “Organizing for Change in the 21st Century”)

[AR] Resilience requires more than forecasting a single future. The text argues for modularity, social cohesion, awareness of affected communities, foresight, scanning, innovation, and experimentation across multiple possible futures. (Ch. 15, “Organizing for Change in the 21st Century”)

[AP] Organizations are increasingly evaluated for social impact as well as financial and product performance. The social-enterprise conception combines revenue and profit with responsibility to employees, communities, environments, and stakeholder networks. (Ch. 15, “Organizing for Change in the 21st Century”)

---

## 16. Organizational structure and change

### Structure, design, and informal organization

[AP] Organizational structure connects work activities; organizational design establishes structures suited to organizational needs; organizational change describes continuing shifts in the system; managed change intentionally shapes those shifts. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Structures and Design”)

[AP] Organizational development is a field of change management that applies social science to organizational performance, employee well-being, and sustainable social benefit. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Structures and Design”)

[AP] The formal organization defines official relationships, responsibilities, communication, and accountability. The informal organization is the emergent network through which people actually interact and exert influence. Either can support or obstruct the other. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Structures and Design”)

[BT] Max Weber’s bureaucratic model is presented through specialization, command-and-control, span of control, centralization, and formalization. These elements can be configured more or less mechanistically. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Structures and Design”)

[AP] Mechanistic bureaucracy emphasizes hierarchy, formalization, centralized decisions, narrow specialization, and routine. Organic bureaucracy relies more on self-organization, decentralization, broad roles, horizontal relationships, and local adaptation. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Structures and Design”)

[AR] Neither pole is inherently superior. Innovation and ambiguous environments favour organic features; consistency, reliability, and tightly controlled work may favour mechanistic features. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Structures and Design”)

### Forms and evolution of change

[AP] Structural change alters formal relationships; technological change introduces tools or systems that often require new relationships; culture change reshapes assumptions and organizational identity and commonly requires years. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Change”)

[AP] The organizational life cycle has four phases: entrepreneurship; survival and early success; sustained success or maturity; and renewal or decline. Growth generally creates pressure for differentiation, formalization, hierarchy, and later rebalancing between control and adaptability. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Change”)

[AP] Change has three dimensions: scope, level, and intentionality. Scope ranges from incremental to transformational and includes strategically directed change; level may be individual, group, or organization-wide; intentionality distinguishes planned from unplanned change. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Change”)

[AR] Higher-level change usually requires supporting changes below it. An organization-wide strategy cannot be implemented without corresponding team relationships and individual knowledge or behaviour. (Ch. 16, “Organizational Change”)

### Assumptions and change models

[AP] Change management is the process of designing and implementing change. The chosen methodology should match the situation because every model has strengths and limitations. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[AP] Three diagnostic questions ask whether change begins from deficiency or abundance, whether it will be imposed top-down or emerge bottom-up, and whether leaders hold a conventional or appreciative view of people. Real interventions often combine these positions. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[AR] Top-down change uses formal authority and can provide clarity and scale; bottom-up change increases participation and emergent adaptation. The more complex the prospective change, the stronger the text’s case for involving affected employees. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[BT] Kurt Lewin’s model moves through unfreezing existing routines, changing to a new state, and refreezing new norms. The text notes that permanent refreezing fits stable contexts better than environments of continuous change. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[BT] John Kotter’s eight-step model establishes urgency, creates a guiding coalition, develops a vision, communicates it, removes obstacles, creates small wins, consolidates improvements, and anchors change. It is especially compatible with formal, hierarchical, top-down change. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[BT] David Cooperrider’s Appreciative Inquiry is presented as abundance-based, participatory, bottom-up, and positive. Its 5-D cycle is define, discover, dream, design, and destiny. Dialogue changes organizational narratives while building relationships and collective capacity. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[BT] The complex-adaptive-systems model is associated with Olson and Eoyang. It treats organizations as continually adapting systems whose exact responses are emergent and cannot be fully predicted or controlled. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[AP] From this perspective, leaders facilitate relationships and conditions for self-organization. They examine employee agency, interpersonal connection, and flows of information and energy, and can influence boundary conditions, introduce constructive disturbances, and create transformational connections. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[AE] Open Space Technology illustrates emergent change: participants propose questions, construct an agenda, join the conversations they consider valuable, and formulate actions without a fully predetermined programme. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

[AR] The models are not mutually exclusive. Kotter can frame an extended programme while Appreciative Inquiry or Open Space supplies participatory work within particular stages. (Ch. 16, “Managing Change”)

## 17. Human resource management

### Strategic role and employee life cycle

[BT] The chapter uses Ulrich, Younger, Brockbank, and Younger’s four waves of HR: administrative delivery and compliance; design of specialist HR practices; integration with business strategy; and an outside-in focus on customers, investors, communities, and reputation. (Ch. 17, “An Introduction to Human Resource Management”)

[AP] Human resource management coordinates the employee life cycle from recruitment and onboarding through performance, development, internal movement, retention, and separation. Human capital is treated as a source of organizational capability and competitive advantage. (Ch. 17, “An Introduction to Human Resource Management”)

[AP] Five core process areas are HR compliance; selection, hiring, and onboarding; performance management; compensation, rewards, and benefits; and talent development and succession planning. (Ch. 17, “An Introduction to Human Resource Management”)

### Compliance and performance management

[AP] HR compliance protects employees and the organization from legal, financial, and reputational harm. The chapter’s principal statutory list covers ADEA, ADA, FLSA, FMLA, NLRA, and WARN. (Ch. 17, “Human Resource Management and Compliance”)

[AP] Education and training, maintained documentation such as employee handbooks, legal review, and recurring audits are presented as complementary controls. Laws and guidance change, so compliance is an ongoing capability rather than a one-time checklist. (Ch. 17, “Human Resource Management and Compliance”)

[AR] Performance management is a business process jointly enacted by HR and line managers. HR designs and facilitates the system, while managers observe, communicate, document, develop, and respond to performance. (Ch. 17, “Performance Management”)

[AP] Forced ranking sharpened distinctions but fostered internal competition and weakened collaboration. Newer approaches favour frequent, forward-looking, individualized feedback, yet complete removal of evaluation can also leave employees without fairness, differentiation, or guidance. (Ch. 17, “Performance Management”)

[AP] Persistent design challenges include aligning individual and organizational goals, connecting rewards to performance, addressing poor performance in real time, managing legal risk, and collecting useful feedback without creating an unmanageable “firehose.” (Ch. 17, “Performance Management”)

### Rewards, acquisition, and development

[AP] Pay-for-performance systems differentiate compensation according to contribution. Implementation requires an agreed philosophy, financial analysis, diagnosis of process gaps, redesigned compensation mechanisms, and communication and training. (Ch. 17, “Influencing Employee Performance and Motivation”)

[AP] The total-rewards model has six elements: compensation, benefits, work–life effectiveness, recognition, performance management, and talent development. (Ch. 17, “Influencing Employee Performance and Motivation”)

[BT] Nohria, Groysberg, and Lee’s model identifies drives to acquire, bond, comprehend, and defend. Corresponding organizational levers include rewards, culture, job design, performance management, and resource-allocation processes. (Ch. 17, “Influencing Employee Performance and Motivation”)

[AP] Talent acquisition establishes the strategy for selection, recruiting, and hiring. A proactive process anticipates leadership requirements, specifies competencies, and develops a sufficiently broad pool before vacancies become emergencies. (Ch. 17, “Building an Organization for the Future”)

[AP] Leadership recruitment proceeds through anticipating needs, specifying the job, developing the pool, assessing candidates, closing the deal, integrating the newcomer, and reviewing the process. Internal ownership remains important even when search work is outsourced. (Ch. 17, “Building an Organization for the Future”)

[AP] Talent development comprises processes for assessing and developing employees. Succession planning identifies critical roles, incumbent risk, and short-, medium-, and long-term successor readiness, including external candidates where internal depth is inadequate. (Ch. 17, “Talent Development and Succession Planning”)

[AP] The 9-box plots performance against potential. Performance refers to results in the current role; potential concerns readiness for higher-level work. Potential is not a measure of a person’s intrinsic value and can change with interest, circumstances, or development. (Ch. 17, “Talent Development and Succession Planning”)

[AP] Talent-review calibration combines multiple leaders’ observations to agree on placement and development. Outputs include identification of high-potential employees, individualized development actions, insight into gaps, and input to succession planning. (Ch. 17, “Talent Development and Succession Planning”)

[AP] Development tools include training, stretch assignments, individual assessments such as 360-degree feedback, and individual development plans. Group-level talent processes should result in individualized action. (Ch. 17, “Talent Development and Succession Planning”)

## 18. Stress and well-being

### Adjustment, stress, and strain

[BT] W. S. Neff’s five work-adjustment profiles describe lack of motivation, fear or anxiety, hostility and aggression, dependency, and social naïveté. The text stresses that maladjustment should not automatically be reduced to laziness or low intelligence. (Ch. 18, “Problems of Work Adjustment”)

[AP] Stress is a physical and emotional reaction to potentially threatening environmental conditions; strain is the resulting psychological or physiological damage. Stress signals a poor fit between demands and the individual’s capacity or resources. (Ch. 18, “Problems of Work Adjustment”)

[AR] Stress is pervasive but not uniform. People interpret the same event differently, and moderate stress can support alertness, motivation, learning, and creativity; intense or prolonged stress produces damage. (Ch. 18, “Problems of Work Adjustment”)

[AP] General adaptation syndrome proceeds through alarm, resistance, and exhaustion. Continued exposure eventually exhausts adaptive capacity and increases vulnerability to illness. (Ch. 18, “Problems of Work Adjustment”)

[AP] Frustration is a reaction to obstruction of goal-directed behaviour. Anxiety is an anticipated inability to cope with future harm, sometimes without a clearly understood cause. (Ch. 18, “Problems of Work Adjustment”)

### Organizational and personal sources

[AP] Four major organizational influences are occupational differences, role ambiguity, role conflict, and role overload or underutilization. High stress is associated particularly with low control, relentless time pressure, threatening conditions, and responsibility for people or major resources. (Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”)

[AP] Role ambiguity reflects inadequate information about expectations, methods, or consequences. Role conflict places contradictory expectations on a person. Role overload exceeds available time or ability, while underutilization leaves important capacities unused. (Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”)

[AR] Quantitative and qualitative workload form separate continua. The best fit occurs when the amount and difficulty of work are reasonably aligned with available time, skill, and capacity; both underload and overload can be harmful. (Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”)

[AP] Three personal influences are personal control, Type A personality, and rate of life change. Participation can increase perceived control, but locus of control affects how people respond when control is restricted. (Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”)

[BT] Friedman and Rosenman’s Type A profile includes impatience, urgency, aggressiveness, competitiveness, simultaneous activity, and heavy work investment; Type B is more deliberate and less driven by time urgency or hostility. (Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”)

[BT] Holmes and Rahe’s life-change work assigns weights to events and argues that accumulated change increases adaptive demand and the probability of illness. The text treats the score probabilistically rather than as a diagnosis. (Ch. 18, “Organizational Influences on Stress”; Appendix B, “Chapter 18”)

### Buffers, outcomes, and coping

[AP] Social support and hardiness buffer the effects of stressors. Social support supplies trust, concern, respect, and practical help; hardiness combines commitment, internal control, and a tendency to treat difficulty as challenge. (Ch. 18, “Buffering Effects of Work related Stress”)

[AP] Four major outcome categories are health effects, counterproductive behaviour, job performance, and burnout. Counterproductive responses include turnover, absenteeism, alcohol or drug misuse, aggression, and sabotage. (Ch. 18, “Buffering Effects of Work related Stress”)

[AR] The stress–performance relationship is described as an inverted J: mild stress may activate performance, while high stress absorbs attention and energy until performance falls sharply. (Ch. 18, “Buffering Effects of Work related Stress”)

[AP] Burnout is exhaustion produced by excessive performance pressure combined with too few sources of satisfaction. It is associated with cynicism, boredom, inadequacy, reduced aspirations, and withdrawal. (Ch. 18, “Buffering Effects of Work related Stress”)

[AP] Individual coping strategies include self-awareness, outside interests, leaving an intolerable organization, personal coping routines, physical exercise, and reframing events according to what is or is not controllable. (Ch. 18, “Coping with Work related Stress”)

[AP] Eight organizational strategies are improved selection and placement, skills training, job redesign, counselling programmes, increased participation and personal control, stronger work-group cohesion, improved communication, and health-promotion programmes. (Ch. 18, “Coping with Work related Stress”)

[AR] Organizational interventions must still fit individual needs. Enrichment can reduce stress for someone seeking autonomy and challenge but increase anxiety when the person does not want the enlarged responsibility. (Ch. 18, “Coping with Work related Stress”)

[BT] The text attributes the term eustress—beneficial stress—and its positive cognitive interpretation to work associated with Richard Lazarus. (Ch. 18, “Coping with Work related Stress”)

## 19. Entrepreneurship

### Forms and stages

[AP] Entrepreneurs recognize and pursue opportunities, accept risk, and convert opportunities into value-producing ventures capable of surviving in a competitive environment. Entrepreneurship can occur in commercial, social, family, technological, or established organizational settings. (Ch. 19, “Overview of Entrepreneurship”)

[BT] The chapter uses Shane and Venkataraman’s field definition: entrepreneurship studies how opportunities are discovered, created, and exploited, by whom, and with what consequences. (Ch. 19, “Overview of Entrepreneurship”)

[AP] Forms discussed are social, corporate, family, serial or habitual, lifestyle, and high-technology entrepreneurship. These classifications concern purpose, organizational setting, ownership, repetition, and growth expectations. (Ch. 19, “Overview of Entrepreneurship”)

[AP] The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor distinguishes potential entrepreneurs, nascent entrepreneurs, new business owners, and established business owners. Total Entrepreneurial Activity counts adults who are nascent entrepreneurs or owner-managers of new businesses. (Ch. 19, “Overview of Entrepreneurship”)

### Entrepreneurial characteristics and capability

[AP] The chapter’s entrepreneurial profile includes ambition, independence, self-confidence, willingness to accept risk, vision, creativity, energy, passion, and commitment. These characteristics do not replace the need for market, technical, and managerial competence. (Ch. 19, “Characteristics of Successful Entrepreneurs”)

[AP] Entrepreneurs need the technical knowledge to implement an idea and the managerial capacity to organize work, establish strategy, obtain finance, communicate, and supervise operations. They must eventually distinguish what they should do themselves from what others should perform. (Ch. 19, “Characteristics of Successful Entrepreneurs”)

### Business models and financing

[BT] Alex Osterwalder and colleagues’ business model canvas describes how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value through customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure. (Ch. 19, “Business Model Canvas”)

[AP] These nine blocks cover four broader areas: customers, the offering, infrastructure, and financial viability. Their value lies in exposing assumptions and dependencies across the whole venture. (Ch. 19, “Business Model Canvas”)

[AE] The Apple example maps a mass-market customer segment, a seamless user proposition, retail and digital channels, brand relationships, hardware and digital revenues, design and marketing activities, content partnerships, and manufacturing and marketing costs. (Ch. 19, “Business Model Canvas”)

[AP] First movers can establish recognition, loyalty, resource positions, and technical standards; second movers can learn from the first entrant and improve the offering. The text reports that either position can prevail. (Ch. 19, “Business Model Canvas”)

[AP] Bootstrapping builds a venture from personal funds or operating revenue. The seven strategies include staying in a known domain, exchanging equity for work, planning around the available budget, deferring office costs, negotiating advances or deferred payments, managing supplier terms, and selecting a cash-flow-favourable business model. (Ch. 19, “New Venture Financing”)

[AP] Debt capital must be repaid under agreed terms; equity capital represents ownership investment without a fixed repayment date. Sources include personal savings, family and friends, angel investors, venture capital, retained earnings, and several forms of bank lending. (Ch. 19, “New Venture Financing”)

[AP] Crowdfunding raises funds from a distributed online audience through reward-based, equity, or debt arrangements. Each form creates a different relationship between backer and venture. (Ch. 19, “New Venture Financing”)

### Design thinking and public support

[AP] Design thinking uses play, empathy, reflection, creation, experimentation, observation, synthesis, feedback, visual representation, and problem solving to navigate uncertain or complex problems. Failure is treated as information for further learning. (Ch. 19, “Design Thinking”)

[AP] Its three phases are inspiration, ideation, and implementation. Divergent thinking expands possibilities; convergent thinking narrows them toward feasible, viable, and desired solutions. (Ch. 19, “Design Thinking”)

[AP] Government can support entrepreneurship by reducing barriers, protecting intellectual property and capital, commercializing public technology, increasing incentives, and selectively supporting industries or regions. The last mechanism carries risks of cronyism and market distortion. (Ch. 19, “Optimal Support for Entrepreneurship”)

[AR] Public support always has trade-offs. Regulation can constrain innovation but also establish predictable rights; public finance can enable risks the private sector avoids but can sustain weak ventures; subsidies can build capacity while diverting resources or favouring connected interests. (Ch. 19, “Optimal Support for Entrepreneurship”)

[AP] Longer-term support includes education, financial literacy, incubators, networking, early exposure to entrepreneurial examples, non-discrimination, and institutions that make knowledge, capital, and relationships more accessible. (Ch. 19, “Optimal Support for Entrepreneurship”)
